Title: Barracuda links cloud breach to ARTEX AI-powered cyberattack
Context: According to the cybersecurity company, the attacker reached a system that stores customer integration credentials for Barracuda XDR; however, it found no evidence that those...
Full Text:
Hackers who breached the cloud environment of network and email security company Barracuda earlier this month used a stolen cloud access key and the ARTEX AI penetration testing framework.

The company says the attacker accessed approximately 10 of its cloud accounts over a 44-hour period between November 1 and 2.

The attacker's presence was discovered on November 4, and Barracuda's investigation determined that the open-source AI pentesting framework ARTEX was used for this "machine-speed intrusion."

The company explains that the attacker leveraged a cloud access key provided to a third-party vendor for the duration of a previous project.

"We did not retire the key when the vendor — a company working in AI — finished that work. That is on us," Barracuda says.

The security company believes the attacker stole the key from the unnamed third-party AI vendor in October. It confirmed that the key was stored in a configuration file in the vendor's GitHub repository.

The attacker used credentials they found in one system to move through Barracuda’s data analytics environment, source-code repositories, and Kubernetes clusters.

Based on the attacker's commands targeting cryptocurrency-related secrets, including private keys, Ethereum keystore files, and seed phrases, Barracuda believes the attack was financially motivated.

However, the company does not rule out that this activity might have been a diversion from the attacker’s true motive.

The threat actor attempted to establish persistence by deploying a container that mounted the host’s file system, including credentials stored on it.

A separate attempt to create a new cloud administrator identity was blocked.

Barracuda says the attack used machine-style labels, certain probing methods, and built-in hunting routines that matched what is found in ARTEX.

The firm noted that the attack was very similar to a recent incident at cloud hosting provider Railway, which also involved credential chaining and the apparent use of ARTEX.

According to the cybersecurity company, the attacker reached a system that stores customer integration credentials for Barracuda XDR; however, it found no evidence that those were accessed or stolen.

Because of the uncertainty surrounding this scenario, Barracuda asked potentially affected Managed XDR Cloud or Monitored Endpoint customers to revoke and recreate their integration credentials.

Barracuda assures customers who did not receive direct communications about this incident that they need to take no action.

Title: Barracuda Hacked Amid Surge in Artex-Powered Cyberattacks
Context: Artex was designed for security testing, but threat actors have been using it as part of in-the-wild intrusions since at least August, and its occurrence in real-world attacks...
Full Text:
The Artex agentic AI penetration testing framework has become a common tool in Chinese threat actors’ arsenal, and Barracuda is one of its victims.

Published on GitHub in July 2026, Artex relies on a planner to formulate an objective and create tasks based on it, and on agents to perform those tasks, while the platform itself records the progress, findings, and assets.

It reportedly used DeepSeek v4.1-flash as the initial model, but can use other LLMs as well, and GLM-5.3 and Grok 4.6 were observed in certain instances. Overall, however, its users mainly rely on Chinese models, which are more permissive compared to US-made ones.

Artex was designed for security testing, but threat actors have been using it as part of in-the-wild intrusions since at least August, and its occurrence in real-world attacks has increased significantly during the past several weeks.

“The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale,” the FBI warns in a new alert (PDF).

Mentioning the framework’s use in attacks on South Korean financial firms and ConnectWise, the FBI warns of the risks Artex poses: faster attacks through automation, exploitation of neglected peripheral devices, and the ability to find and exploit supply chain attack vectors.

The framework’s developer removed their GitHub repository in October, but Artex continues to proliferate through other channels. In early November, Censys was seeing roughly 1,500 hosts running exposed Artex consoles.

In October, Artex was used by Chinese espionage group Vapor Panda in a campaign targeting over 200 organizations in 14 countries, including “foreign ministries, a European presidency, and US pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defense, and nuclear organizations,” SentinelOne reports.

Storm-0940 is another Chinese state-sponsored group using Artex, but evidence shows that financially motivated threat actors such as Storm-3358 have also adopted the framework, Cisco’s Talos notes.

Post-exploitation, the threat actors were seen abusing compromised credentials and keys, escalating privileges, deploying persistence, moving laterally, and stealing credentials and data.

“Observed impacts range from access to cloud secrets and mailbox data to the use of compromised applications to reach connected environments,” Talos says.

Amazon describes similar observations, noting that one of the most prominent Artex campaigns was focused on large-scale theft of credentials to access AI models, while another targeted cryptocurrency exchanges.

Barracuda, which fell victim to an Artex-powered intrusion, published similar findings: hackers used an exposed valid cloud access key to map its reach, then reused discovered secrets to access more systems and exfiltrate more credentials and secrets.

“In all, the attacker touched about 10 cloud accounts in roughly 44 hours. The work was methodical and tireless. The probe names, the other indicators we collected, the order in which the attacker worked through our systems, and its built-in routines for hunting credentials and wallets all match Artex,” Barracuda explains.

The attack unfolded between November 1 and November 2, targeted sensitive material across secret stores, configurations, Kubernetes service accounts, and server metadata services, and left a backdoor behind in a Kubernetes cluster.

On some servers, the attackers gained shell access and used it to search for Ethereum keystore files, seed phrase files, extended private keys, and other wallet-related information.

The attack, Barracuda says, was similar to the October intrusion at cloud application hosting platform Railway. Furthermore, it fits the previously reported wave of intrusions at dozens of AI developer platforms.

Barracuda has not attributed the attack, noting that Artex is used by many groups.

Amazon’s analysis of two Artex-powered campaigns revealed that the attackers relied on long-known techniques, but operated at far greater speeds courtesy of AI.

“The agents succeeded where basic security hygiene was missing, including default or hardcoded credentials, keys left in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software. Getting those fundamentals right remains the most effective defense,” Amazon says.

“The reported Artex activity shows that autonomous attackers don’t need a zero-day. They can find exposed services, exploit authorization gaps, and keep adapting while defenders are still triaging alerts and approving a response. When every defensive action has to wait for a person, the attacker controls the pace. Defenders need to move from identifying exposure to verified protection at machine speed,” Miggo Security co-founder and CEO Daniel Shechter said.

Title: Barracuda’s email security gateways bitten by make-me-root vulns
Context: Security company Barracuda warns that attackers are exploiting a pre-authentication authorization bypass bug and a command-injection vulnerability in its popular Email Security...
Full Text: Security company Barracuda warns that attackers are exploiting a pre-authentication authorization bypass bug and a command-injection vulnerability in its popular Email Security Gateway (ESG) products that, when chained, could allow the crims to run commands with root privileges. “We have identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations,” the security vendor said in a late Monday night update to its earlier security advisory. Barracuda declined to answer The Register’s questions, including one about how many organizations have been hit by attackers. A company spokesperson told us that it “worked directly” with the affected businesses “to quickly address the issue. Barracuda acted promptly to remediate the vulnerabilities, releasing patches for affected products.” The vendor disclosed and fixed the vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, last week. CVE-2026-116606 is a 9.3 CVSS-rated, pre-authentication authorization bypass flaw in ESG. While authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability, the attacker must have access to the administrative user interface. As Purplecop Security founder Tausif Ahmed said on Tuesday: “If your Email Security Gateway's admin UI is open to the internet, that's the first thing I'd close today.” CVE-2026-111560 is an 8.6-rated command-injection flaw that affects multiple Barracuda products: its ESG, load balancer (ADC), message archiver (BMA), web application firewall (WAF), WAF control center (WCC), and web security gateway (WSG). “If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device,” Barracuda warned on November 2. At the time, the vendor did not report any active exploitation of either. We don’t yet know who is responsible for the attacks, or whether the intruders gained root access – but if they did, they could steal data, install backdoors, and take full control of affected systems. These types of edge-device exploits have been used by Chinese-government spies, and in 2023 the FBI blamed PRC-linked attackers for a series of attacks that targeted Barracuda ESGs to deploy custom malware and maintain access to high-value networks. According to Mandiant, 27 percent of identified affected organizations were government entities. So if you haven’t already: patch now. ®
